claim: TMEM16 proteins and OSCA/TMEM63 proteins belong to the Transmembrane Channel/Scramblase (TCS) superfamily.
source: The calcium-activated TMEM16 proteins and the mechanosensitive/osmolarity-activated OSCA/TMEM63 proteins belong to the Transmembrane Channel/Scramblase (TCS) superfamily.
evidence: This is stated directly in the abstract and is supported by established scientific classification of these protein families.

claim: OSCA/TMEM63 proteins function solely as ion channels.
source: Within the superfamily, OSCA/TMEM63 proteins, as well as TMEM16A and TMEM16B, are thought to function solely as ion channels.
evidence: This represents the current understanding in the field prior to the findings of this study.

claim: TMEM16A and TMEM16B function solely as ion channels.
source: Within the superfamily, OSCA/TMEM63 proteins, as well as TMEM16A and TMEM16B, are thought to function solely as ion channels.
evidence: This represents the current understanding in the field prior to the findings of this study.

claim: Most TMEM16 members maintain an additional function as scramblases.
source: However, most TMEM16 members, including TMEM16F, maintain an additional function as scramblases, rapidly exchanging phospholipids between leaflets of the membrane.
evidence: This is supported by previous research on TMEM16 family members.

claim: TMEM16F functions as a scramblase that rapidly exchanges phospholipids between membrane leaflets.
source: However, most TMEM16 members, including TMEM16F, maintain an additional function as scramblases, rapidly exchanging phospholipids between leaflets of the membrane.
evidence: This is supported by previous research on TMEM16F.

claim: Single mutations along the TM 4/6 interface allow non-scrambling TCS members to permeate phospholipids.
source: Here, we show that single mutations along the transmembrane helix (TM) 4/6 interface allow non-scrambling TCS members to permeate phospholipids.
evidence: This is a primary finding of the study supported by experimental data presented in the manuscript.

claim: TM 4 plays a key role in controlling TCS ion and lipid permeation.
source: In particular, this study highlights the key role of TM 4 in controlling TCS ion and lipid permeation and offers novel insights into the evolution of the TCS superfamily, suggesting that, like TMEM16s, the OSCA/TMEM63 family maintains a conserved potential to permeate ions and phospholipids.
evidence: This is a primary conclusion of the study based on experimental data showing effects of TM 4 mutations.

claim: The OSCA/TMEM63 family maintains a conserved potential to permeate ions and phospholipids.
source: In particular, this study highlights the key role of TM 4 in controlling TCS ion and lipid permeation and offers novel insights into the evolution of the TCS superfamily, suggesting that, like TMEM16s, the OSCA/TMEM63 family maintains a conserved potential to permeate ions and phospholipids.
evidence: This is a primary conclusion of the study based on experimental data showing that mutations can convert OSCA/TMEM63 proteins into scramblases.

claim: TMEM16 CaPLSases have roles in blood coagulation.
source: Discoveries of two scramblase families—the TMEM16 calcium-activated phospholipid scramblases (CaPLSases) and XKR caspase-dependent phospholipid scramblases—have revealed roles for scramblases in processes such as blood coagulation (Suzuki et al., 2010; Yang et al., 2012; Fujii et al., 2015), angiogenesis (Shan et al., 2024), cell death signaling (Kunzelmann et al., 2019; Suzuki et al., 2013a), phagocytosis (Suzuki et al., 2013a), cell migration (Jacobsen et al., 2013; Chang et al., 2017), membrane repair (Griffin et al., 2016; Chandra et al., 2019), microparticle release (Fujii et al., 2015), cell–cell fusion (Whitlock et al., 2018; Zhang et al., 2020; Zhang et al., 2022), and viral infection (Zaitseva et al., 2017; Nanbo et al., 2018).
evidence: This is supported by cited references to previous studies.

claim: The TMEM16 family was originally classified as calcium-activated chloride channels based on TMEM16A and TMEM16B.
source: The TMEM16 family (Figure 1—figure supplement 1) was originally classified as calcium-activated chloride channels (CaCCs) based on the first-discovered members, TMEM16A and TMEM16B (Caputo et al., 2008; Yang et al., 2008; Schroeder et al., 2008).
evidence: This is supported by cited references to the original discovery papers.

claim: TMEM16F represents the canonical CaPLSase.
source: Most remaining members, however, exhibit CaPLSase activity, with TMEM16F representing the canonical CaPLSase (Suzuki et al., 2013b; Figure 1a).
evidence: This is supported by cited references and illustrated in Figure 1a.

claim: CaPLSases function as non-selective ion channels along with their non-specific permeability to phospholipids.
source: Uniquely, CaPLSases also function as non-selective ion channels along with their non-specific permeability to phospholipids (Yang et al., 2012; Grubb et al., 2013; Wong et al., 2013; Yu et al., 2015; Di Zanni et al., 2018; Le et al., 2019b).
evidence: This is supported by multiple cited references.

claim: Calcium-induced conformational changes cause clamshell-like separation of TMs 4 and 6 to facilitate ion and phospholipid permeation.
source: Substrate permeation is facilitated by calcium-induced conformational changes causing the clamshell-like separation of TMs 4 and 6 to facilitate ion and phospholipid permeation (Le et al., 2019a; Lam et al., 2021; Lam and Dutzler, 2021; Figure 1—figure supplement 1b–d).
evidence: This is supported by cited references and illustrated in Figure 1—figure supplement 1b–d.

claim: Conformational changes catalyze phospholipid permeation by thinning the membrane near the permeation pathway.
source: These conformational changes further catalyzed phospholipid permeation by thinning the membrane near the permeation pathway (Falzone et al., 2019; Falzone et al., 2022).
evidence: This is supported by cited references.

claim: The TMEM16 family together with the OSCA/TMEM63 family and TMC family collectively form the Transmembrane Channel/Scramblase (TCS) superfamily.
source: The TMEM16 family together with the OSCA/TMEM63 family and TMC family (Keresztes et al., 2003; Hahn et al., 2009; Medrano-Soto et al., 2018; Ballesteros et al., 2018) collectively form the Transmembrane Channel/Scramblase (TCS) superfamily (Le et al., 2021).
evidence: This is supported by cited references.

claim: The TCS superfamily has a conserved 10-TM architectural core.
source: Despite the conserved 10-TM architectural core (Jojoa-Cruz et al., 2018; Liu et al., 2018; Zhang et al., 2018; Maity et al., 2019; Jeong et al., 2022), phospholipid permeability has not been experimentally demonstrated in mechanosensitive OSCA/TMEM63 or TMC proteins, raising the intriguing question of how TCS proteins discriminate between ion and ion/phospholipid substrates.
evidence: This is supported by cited references.

claim: Phospholipid permeability has not been experimentally demonstrated in mechanosensitive OSCA/TMEM63 or TMC proteins.
source: Despite the conserved 10-TM architectural core (Jojoa-Cruz et al., 2018; Liu et al., 2018; Zhang et al., 2018; Maity et al., 2019; Jeong et al., 2022), phospholipid permeability has not been experimentally demonstrated in mechanosensitive OSCA/TMEM63 or TMC proteins, raising the intriguing question of how TCS proteins discriminate between ion and ion/phospholipid substrates.
evidence: This represents the state of knowledge prior to this study.

claim: TMEM16A CaCC can be genetically modified to enable phospholipid permeability by substituting TMEM16F domains as small as 15 amino acids.
source: Interestingly, studies have shown that the TMEM16A CaCC can be genetically modified to enable phospholipid permeability, either by substituting TMEM16F domains as small as 15 amino acids (Yu et al., 2015), or through single mutations at the hydrophobic gate (Le et al., 2019a).
evidence: This is supported by cited references.

claim: TMEM16A CaCC can be genetically modified to enable phospholipid permeability through single mutations at the hydrophobic gate.
source: Interestingly, studies have shown that the TMEM16A CaCC can be genetically modified to enable phospholipid permeability, either by substituting TMEM16F domains as small as 15 amino acids (Yu et al., 2015), or through single mutations at the hydrophobic gate (Le et al., 2019a).
evidence: This is supported by cited references.

claim: TMEM16F I521K causes spontaneous, global exposure of PS on the plasma membrane without requiring calcium stimulation.
source: Similar to TMEM16F F518K (Le et al., 2019a), overexpressing the single lysine mutations TMEM16F I521K and M522K led to spontaneous, global exposure of PS on the plasma membrane without requiring calcium stimulation (Figure 1b, c).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1b, c.

claim: TMEM16F M522K causes spontaneous, global exposure of PS on the plasma membrane without requiring calcium stimulation.
source: Similar to TMEM16F F518K (Le et al., 2019a), overexpressing the single lysine mutations TMEM16F I521K and M522K led to spontaneous, global exposure of PS on the plasma membrane without requiring calcium stimulation (Figure 1b, c).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1b, c.

claim: TMEM16F T526K causes minimal spontaneous PS exposure.
source: In contrast, T526K, which is one helical turn below I521 and M522 (Figure 1a), caused minimal spontaneous PS exposure (Figure 1b, c).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1b, c.

claim: TMEM16F I521K shows robust depolarization-activated outward rectifying currents in the absence of calcium.
source: In the absence of calcium, I521K and M522K, but not WT TMEM16F or T526K, showed robust depolarization-activated outward rectifying currents (Figure 1d–f).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1d–f.

claim: TMEM16F M522K shows robust depolarization-activated outward rectifying currents in the absence of calcium.
source: In the absence of calcium, I521K and M522K, but not WT TMEM16F or T526K, showed robust depolarization-activated outward rectifying currents (Figure 1d–f).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1d–f.

claim: TMEM16F WT does not show robust depolarization-activated outward rectifying currents in the absence of calcium.
source: In the absence of calcium, I521K and M522K, but not WT TMEM16F or T526K, showed robust depolarization-activated outward rectifying currents (Figure 1d–f).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1d–f.

claim: TMEM16F T526K does not show robust depolarization-activated outward rectifying currents in the absence of calcium.
source: In the absence of calcium, I521K and M522K, but not WT TMEM16F or T526K, showed robust depolarization-activated outward rectifying currents (Figure 1d–f).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1d–f.

claim: TMEM16F I521E leads to spontaneous, global PS exposure in all transfected cells.
source: I521E led to spontaneous, global PS exposure in all transfected cells, whereas I521A failed to cause spontaneous PS exposure (Figure 1—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 2.

claim: TMEM16F I521A fails to cause spontaneous PS exposure.
source: I521E led to spontaneous, global PS exposure in all transfected cells, whereas I521A failed to cause spontaneous PS exposure (Figure 1—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 2.

claim: TMEM16F I611K results in spontaneous, global PS exposure.
source: Comparable to I521K (Figure 1b, c), I521E (Figure 1—figure supplement 2), and M522K (Figure 1b, c), I611K resulted in spontaneous, global PS exposure (Figure 2b, c).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2b, c.

claim: TMEM16F I611K-expressing cells exhibit robust, depolarization-activated outward rectifying currents in the absence of calcium.
source: Likewise, I611K-expressing cells exhibited robust, depolarization-activated outward rectifying currents in the absence of calcium (Figure 2d–f).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2d–f.

claim: TMEM16A I546K-expressing cells exhibit spontaneous, global PS exposure.
source: Similar to TMEM16A L543K (Le et al., 2019a), I546K- and I547K-expressing cells exhibit spontaneous, global PS exposure (Figure 3b, c), analogous to the equivalent TMEM16F mutations I521K and M522K (Figure 1—figure supplement 1f; Figure 1b, c).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3b, c.

claim: TMEM16A I547K-expressing cells exhibit spontaneous, global PS exposure.
source: Similar to TMEM16A L543K (Le et al., 2019a), I546K- and I547K-expressing cells exhibit spontaneous, global PS exposure (Figure 3b, c), analogous to the equivalent TMEM16F mutations I521K and M522K (Figure 1—figure supplement 1f; Figure 1b, c).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3b, c.

claim: TMEM16A I546K and I547K show GOF ion channel activity at depolarizing potentials in the absence of calcium stimulation.
source: Similarly, whole-cell patch clamp revealed GOF ion channel activity at depolarizing potentials, even in the absence of calcium stimulation (Figure 3d–f).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3d–f.

claim: TMEM16A E551K fails to exhibit PS exposure.
source: In contrast, E551K, equivalent to T526K in TMEM16F, failed to exhibit PS exposure, but showed modest ion channel activity at depolarizing potentials in the absence of calcium, perhaps reflecting the gate is open sufficiently for ion but not phospholipid permeation.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data.

claim: TMEM16A E551K shows modest ion channel activity at depolarizing potentials in the absence of calcium.
source: In contrast, E551K, equivalent to T526K in TMEM16F, failed to exhibit PS exposure, but showed modest ion channel activity at depolarizing potentials in the absence of calcium, perhaps reflecting the gate is open sufficiently for ion but not phospholipid permeation.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data.

claim: Ani9 at 10 µM prevents spontaneous PS exposure for TMEM16A I546K.
source: Similar to our previous observation of TMEM16A L543K (Le et al., 2019a), chronic incubation of Ani9 at 10 μM also prevented spontaneous PS exposure for I546K (Figure 3—figure supplement 1d).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1d.

claim: 10 μM Ani9 reversibly inhibits voltage-elicited TMEM16A I546K currents by over 50%.
source: Interestingly, 10 μM Ani9 reversibly inhibited voltage-elicited TMEM16A I546K currents by over 50% (Figure 3—figure supplement 1a–c).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1a–c.

claim: OSCA1.2 was first discovered in plants as a family of mechanosensitive and osmolarity-activated cation non-selective ion channels.
source: We next applied our approach to a TMEM16 relative from the OSCA/TMEM63 family (Figure 1—figure supplement 1a), which was first discovered in plants as a family of mechanosensitive and osmolarity-activated cation non-selective ion channels (Yuan et al., 2014; Figure 4a).
evidence: This is supported by cited reference.

claim: OSCA1.2 WT lacks spontaneous phospholipid scramblase activity.
source: Overexpressing eGFP-tagged OSCA1.2 WT in TMEM16F KO HEK293T cells did not induce PS exposure, demonstrating that OSCA1.2 WT lacks spontaneous phospholipid scramblase activity (Figure 4b).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4b.

claim: OSCA1.2 L438K causes cells to exhibit spontaneous and global PS exposure.
source: Strikingly, a single-point mutation, L438K, causes cells overexpressing the OSCA1.2 mutant to exhibit spontaneous and global PS exposure (Figure 4b, c).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4b, c.

claim: OSCA1.2 L438K significantly left-shifts the conductance–voltage (G–V) relationship compared to WT.
source: We found that the mutant significantly left-shifts the conductance–voltage (G–V) relationship (Figure 4e, f) and accelerates channel activation kinetics (Figure 4g) compared to WT.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4e, f.

claim: OSCA1.2 L438K accelerates channel activation kinetics compared to WT.
source: We found that the mutant significantly left-shifts the conductance–voltage (G–V) relationship (Figure 4e, f) and accelerates channel activation kinetics (Figure 4g) compared to WT.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4g.

claim: Under −50 mmHg of pressure, OSCA1.2 L438K has a half-maximal voltage (V0.5) of 66.7 ± 3.7 mV.
source: Under −50 mmHg of pressure, L438K has a half-maximal voltage (V0.5) of 66.7 ± 3.7 mV, while the WT V0.5 is nearly 108.7 ± 5.6 mV (Figure 4f), underscoring that this mutation also promotes channel gating.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4f.

claim: Under −50 mmHg of pressure, OSCA1.2 WT has a half-maximal voltage (V0.5) of nearly 108.7 ± 5.6 mV.
source: Under −50 mmHg of pressure, L438K has a half-maximal voltage (V0.5) of 66.7 ± 3.7 mV, while the WT V0.5 is nearly 108.7 ± 5.6 mV (Figure 4f), underscoring that this mutation also promotes channel gating.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4f.

claim: The OSCA1.2 L438K trajectory showed considerably increased hydration of the pore region compared to WT.
source: Remarkably, the L438K trajectory showed considerably increased hydration of the pore region compared to WT (Figure 4—figure supplement 1b).
evidence: This is supported by MD simulation data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1b.

claim: Enhanced hydration in OSCA1.2 L438K is attributed to a modest expansion of the TM 4/6 interface throughout the simulation.
source: This enhanced hydration is attributed to a modest expansion of the TM 4/6 interface throughout the simulation (Figure 4—figure supplement 1a).
evidence: This is supported by MD simulation data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1a.

claim: OSCA1.2 K435L/L438K results in a modest level of spontaneous PS exposure (31%).
source: Remarkably, the double mutant K435L/L438K, which shifts the lysine to position 438, resulted in a modest level of spontaneous PS exposure (31%, Figure 4—figure supplement 2b, c).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 2b, c.

claim: OSCA1.2 K435L does not induce significant spontaneous PS exposure (3%).
source: In contrast, K435L (L435/L438) did not induce significant spontaneous PS exposure (3%, Figure 4—figure supplement 2b, c).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 2b, c.

claim: OSCA1.2 A439K results in minimal spontaneous PS exposure (10%).
source: Interestingly, mutating the neighboring amino acid (Figure 4a), A439, to lysine resulted in minimal spontaneous PS exposure (10%, Figure 4b, c).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4b, c.

claim: PS exposure is robustly induced for OSCA1.2 A439K in response to hypotonic stimulation.
source: Indeed, PS exposure was robustly induced for the A439K mutant (Figure 5b, c) but not WT (Figure 5a, c) in response to hypotonic stimulation.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5b, c.

claim: PS exposure is not robustly induced for OSCA1.2 WT in response to hypotonic stimulation.
source: Indeed, PS exposure was robustly induced for the A439K mutant (Figure 5b, c) but not WT (Figure 5a, c) in response to hypotonic stimulation.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5a, c.

claim: OSCA1.2 A439K enhances ion channel activity as evidenced by accelerated activation kinetics.
source: Inside-out patch clamp further demonstrated that A439K enhances OSCA1.2 ion channel activity as evidenced by the accelerated activation kinetics (Figure 4g) and left-shifted G–V relationship (Figure 4f).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4g.

claim: OSCA1.2 A439K enhances ion channel activity as evidenced by left-shifted G–V relationship.
source: Inside-out patch clamp further demonstrated that A439K enhances OSCA1.2 ion channel activity as evidenced by the accelerated activation kinetics (Figure 4g) and left-shifted G–V relationship (Figure 4f).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4f.

claim: TMEM63s represent the mammalian members of the OSCA/TMEM63 family with three members present in humans (TMEM63A–C).
source: TMEM63s represent the mammalian members of the OSCA/TMEM63 family with three members present in humans (TMEM63A–C).
evidence: This is established knowledge about the TMEM63 family.

claim: TMEM63s function as mechanosensitive ion channels gated by high-threshold membrane tension.
source: Recent structural and functional characterizations indicate that TMEM63s function as mechanosensitive ion channels gated by high-threshold membrane tension and, in notable contrast to all other structurally resolved TCS superfamily members, they likely function as monomers (Zheng et al., 2023; Qin et al., 2023; Wu et al., 2024).
evidence: This is supported by cited references.

claim: TMEM63s likely function as monomers.
source: Recent structural and functional characterizations indicate that TMEM63s function as mechanosensitive ion channels gated by high-threshold membrane tension and, in notable contrast to all other structurally resolved TCS superfamily members, they likely function as monomers (Zheng et al., 2023; Qin et al., 2023; Wu et al., 2024).
evidence: This is supported by cited references.

claim: Overexpressing mouse TMEM63A with single lysine mutations at W472 leads to spontaneous PS exposure.
source: Indeed, overexpressing eGFP-tagged mouse TMEM63A with single lysine mutations at either W472 or S475 led to spontaneous PS exposure (Figure 6b, c), though the AnV staining revealed punctate rather than global patterns of PS exposure induced by their OSCA1.2 counterparts.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 6b, c.

claim: Overexpressing mouse TMEM63A with single lysine mutations at S475 leads to spontaneous PS exposure.
source: Indeed, overexpressing eGFP-tagged mouse TMEM63A with single lysine mutations at either W472 or S475 led to spontaneous PS exposure (Figure 6b, c), though the AnV staining revealed punctate rather than global patterns of PS exposure induced by their OSCA1.2 counterparts.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 6b, c.

claim: TMEM63A A476K fails to show obvious PS exposure.
source: Notably, A476K failed to show obvious PS exposure (Figure 6b, c), even after 120 mOsm/kg hypotonic treatment (Figure 6—figure supplement 1b, c), perhaps reflecting differences in mechanical pressure threshold between OSCA1.2 and TMEM63A (Zheng et al., 2023).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 6b, c and Figure 6—figure supplement 1b, c.

claim: TMEM63A W472K, S475K, and A476K cause marked reductions in V0.5 from 122.3 ± 3.5 mV for WT to 95.9 ± 6.3, 92.1 ± 8.6, and 96.8 ± 4.2 mV, respectively.
source: W472K, S475K, and A476K caused marked reductions in V0.5 from 122.3 ± 3.5 mV for WT to 95.9 ± 6.3, 92.1 ± 8.6, and 96.8 ± 4.2 mV, respectively (Figure 6d–f).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 6d–f.

claim: Lysine is above only arginine on the hydropathy index.
source: Lysine is above only arginine on the hydropathy index and thus likely explains why it readily destabilizes the gate.
evidence: This is based on established knowledge of amino acid hydropathy.
